voice: An educated, imposing Cairo Museum envoy: fiercely committed to repatriation, vain, patriarchal, and ominously theatrical, without exoticist mysticism or jokes at the expense of Egyptian identity.

entries.text: I have no use for that.
I am not in the mood for idle conversation, Miss Bow.
Dr. Ptahsheptut Smith, of the Cairo Museum. I find it distasteful to celebrate theft in the name of scholarship. The Egyptian artifacts in this museum belong in Egypt.
The museum would say those artifacts were legally acquired.
A legal document can make possession lawful without making it just. Those who profit from Egypt's dead should remember that history has a long memory.
Your admiration is understandable, madam, but kindly refrain from handling the merchandise.
You have already asked me that, Miss Bow.
I do not know that individual.

You dare mention Carter to me? He broke open sacred places, removed the Dagger from Egypt, and called the result scholarship. Men who make enemies of both the living and the dead should not expect peaceful lives.
Do you believe Dr. Carter is in danger?
Carter has earned many enemies. If judgment finds him, whether from a court, a man, or Amon Ra, he will have invited it himself.
Is that a warning?
It is an observation. You may decide how seriously to take it.
I had hoped Dr. Carrington would listen to reason. I arranged another meeting to discuss returning the Dagger to Egypt, but that seems futile now that it is no longer in the museum.
We spoke only by telephone. He denied Egypt's claim to the Dagger. I hoped a personal visit might convince him of our sincerity, but the situation has changed.
O'Riley is investigating the burglary, though the word 'investigating' may be generous. Sobriety might improve his chances.
I do not know Mr. Crodfoller. The name sounds faintly improbable.
I know no one named Lo Fat.
I do not associate with dockworkers, madam.
I have never heard of him.
Heimlich is the tiresome guard who works here. His devotion to security would be admirable if it were accompanied by judgment.
Miss Delacroix is delightful. I have invited her to become my second wife. She has declined with admirable consistency.
You propose to women you barely know?
Only when their qualifications are exceptional.
How discriminating of you.
Your sarcasm is one of your less attractive qualities, Miss Bow.
I am not familiar with that person.
Rameses I founded the Nineteenth Dynasty, though his brief reign was overshadowed by that of Rameses II.
Rameses II commissioned immense building projects whose marks remain across Egypt. His ambition is difficult not to admire.
Najeer? The name is not familiar.
Quite sure. We need not dwell on the matter.
I have met the Countess only briefly, but she appeared sincerely concerned with my difficulties. A charming woman.
Dr. Myklos is highly educated. I would respect her more if she showed proper respect for Egypt's claims.
I represent the Cairo Museum and the people of Egypt. My purpose is to recover what belongs to us, not to Carter or this complacent institution.
I do not know the name.
Bow? The English longbow was decisive at Agincourt despite formidable odds.
Then I have no scholarly opinion about John Bow.
I have never heard of it.
Your police have made very little progress. Cairo's authorities would have questioned every dealer, porter, and shipping agent by now.
You sound very confident in them.
Competence inspires confidence. Detective O'Riley has inspired neither.
I have not been in this country long enough to judge its laundries.
I came through the docks one week ago after crossing from England. Had I known Dr. Carrington was aboard, I would have spoken with him during the voyage.
This could be a fine museum if its management returned the Egyptian collection to its proper home.
New York reminds me of Cairo in its energy and crowds, though it is colder and considerably less patient.
A secret establishment devoted to drinking. Your Prohibition appears to have made alcohol more fashionable than ever.
A diplomat learns not to leave his thoughts lying around. I prefer memory.
I am already aware that you are a journalist.
A handsome pocket watch.
It resembles every other gold pocket watch I have seen.
No.
No. Should it?
How should I know? I am an Egyptologist, not a locksmith.
I prefer mutton.
I am not a common laborer. I handle specialized archaeological instruments.
The Dagger is a profound loss to Egypt: first taken from its temple, then carried out of the country, and now stolen again. When will it finally return home?
No. It is much too small for me.
They have a remarkably strong smell.
Snake oil is an American fraud, is it not? I see no archaeological use for it.
Ruhmkorff lanterns are often used on excavations. They are reliable and, when properly maintained, quite safe.
I am fond of almost every food, but that cheese has announced your arrival from across the room.
That resembles one of Yvette's garters. How curious that you possess it. She gave me one much like it.
Dinosaur bones are outside my field.
I do not recognize it. Some sort of instrument for handling snakes?
I do not know. It appears I have lost the ankh.
I have no interest in Carter's scribblings. Whatever he wrote about Egypt is certain to serve his own reputation.
A magnifying glass is useful, though you should take care what you choose to examine.
A light bulb is useful only when one also has a socket and electricity.
I have no interest in that police file.
It appears to be animal hair.
I have no need of special glasses. My eyesight is excellent.
Those red hairs are plainly not mine.
I can obtain my own drinks, thank you.
It appears useless. Someone has already typed on it.
A woman's shoe. It appears too small for you.
Charcoal is not a subject on which I have an opinion.
Why are you wasting my time with this?
Hieroglyphic writing unites language, image, and ritual. To study it is to hear ancient Egyptians speak in their own words.
No. The treasures of my country's past are leaving Egypt in a flood greater than the Nile.
The Egyptian Antiquities Service approves excavations and the division of finds, doesn't it?
The Service answers too readily to foreign excavators, patrons, and governments. A signature obtained under foreign pressure does not make every removal honorable.
I do not threaten, Miss Bow. I state Egypt's claim plainly and expect civilized institutions to answer it.
No.
It was already stolen once--from Egypt.
Ancient Egyptian history shaped law, religion, architecture, and government across centuries. To treat it merely as a source of curiosities is an insult to scholarship.
Egyptology should be the study of a living country's past, not a license to empty it. Every object here once belonged to a person, a family, a temple, or a tomb.
That sounds as much like advocacy as scholarship.
Scholarship without responsibility is merely grave robbery with footnotes.
And you consider yourself responsible?
More responsible than Carter. I have nothing further to say on the subject.
That holds no interest for me.
Carter broke open sacred places and carried the Dagger out of Egypt. His death does not transform theft into scholarship.
Miss Bow, I am shocked that you would ask. Carter made many enemies; his death proves only that one of them reached him.
Miss Delacroix's death is a genuine loss. She was intelligent, charming, and admirably patient with my proposals. I mourn her.
No, I did not kill her. Your suspicion is considerably less charming than Yvette's company.
At last, a question worthy of the Great Sphinx. Unfortunately, I cannot answer it.
